title: Does a US restaurant need a certified food protection manager under the FDA Food Code?
seoTitle: Food Code certified food manager rules
description: FDA Food Code 2-102.11 and 2-102.12: when the person in charge must be a certified food protection manager, what accreditation counts, and state adoption.
shortAnswer: The FDA Food Code, a model code rather than federal law, says in section 2-102.12 that the person in charge of a food establishment shall be a certified food protection manager who passed a test in an accredited program, and section 2-102.11 requires that person to demonstrate food safety knowledge to inspectors. Whether this binds a given restaurant depends on which Food Code edition, if any, its state or local authority has adopted.
keyTakeaways: The Food Code is a model offered by FDA for adoption by local, state, tribal and federal jurisdictions; it applies to a restaurant only through the rules its regulatory authority has adopted.
Section 2-101.11 requires a person in charge to be present during all hours of operation, and section 2-102.12(A) requires that person to be a certified food protection manager.

Section 2-102.11 lets the person in charge demonstrate knowledge in three ways: no priority item violations, certification, or correct answers to inspector questions across 18 knowledge areas in the 2026 edition.
Section 2-102.20 deems certification compliant when the certifier is accredited by a Conference for Food Protection recognized accrediting agency to the CFP standard.
FDA released the 2026 Food Code on September 17, 2026; it added food defense to the knowledge areas and staff training duties, while 2-102.12 is unchanged.
jurisdiction: United States: FDA Food Code (model code), adopted state by state and locally
regulator: US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) publishes the model; state, local, tribal and territorial regulatory authorities adopt and enforce it
appliesTo: Restaurants, cafeterias and other retail food service establishments in jurisdictions that have adopted the Food Code
Grocery stores and other retail food stores

sections.heading: Is the FDA Food Code legally binding?

blocks.text: Not by itself. FDA describes the [Food Code](https://www.fda.gov/food/retail-food-protection/fda-food-code) as a model that state, local, tribal and federal regulators use to develop or update their own food safety rules, and FDA's 2022 edition page says it is "offered for adoption by local, state, and federal governmental jurisdictions for administration." A restaurant is bound by its own jurisdiction's adopted code, which may be an older edition or a modified version.

FDA moved to a four year publication cycle with the 2005 edition and issues supplements in between. The [2026 edition](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/food-code-2026) is the latest full release, and FDA held a 50 State Call on October 8, 2026 to discuss it and encourage adoption. Because jurisdictions adopt on their own timetables, many will still be enforcing the 2017, 2022 or an earlier edition as at November 2026.

blocks.title: Adoption is state by state
blocks.text: Before relying on any Food Code section, confirm which edition your state, county or city has adopted, any local amendments, and whether manager certification is required for your establishment type. FDA itself notes in Annex 3 that it is appropriate for state and local agencies to set criteria for which establishments are exempt and when more than one certified manager is needed.

sections.heading: What does the Food Code require of the person in charge?

blocks.text: Section 2-101.11(A) requires the permit holder to be the person in charge, or to designate one, and to ensure a person in charge is present at the food establishment during all hours of operation. Section 2-102.12(A) then requires that person in charge to be a certified food protection manager.

blocks.title: Primary text: FDA Food Code 2026, 2-102.12(A)
blocks.text: "The PERSON IN CHARGE shall be a certified FOOD protection manager who has shown proficiency of required information through passing a test that is part of an ACCREDITED PROGRAM."

Paragraph 2-102.12(B) says the requirement does not apply to establishment types the regulatory authority deems to pose minimal risk of causing or contributing to foodborne illness, based on the nature of the operation and extent of food preparation. Read together with 2-101.11, the model code expects a certified manager on site whenever the establishment is open, which is why many operators certify every shift lead rather than a single manager.

sections.heading: How can the person in charge demonstrate knowledge under 2-102.11?

blocks.text: Section 2-102.11 requires the person in charge, during inspections and on request, to demonstrate knowledge of foodborne disease prevention, application of HACCP principles and the Code. It allows three routes, and each is a priority foundation item.

blocks.caption: Three ways to demonstrate knowledge under Food Code 2026, section 2-102.11
head: Paragraph
Route
Practical implication
rows: No violations of priority items during the current inspection
Depends on inspection outcome; cannot be planned for in advance
Being a certified food protection manager who passed a test in an accredited program
The only route that is portable and documented before the inspector arrives
Responding correctly to inspector questions across the listed areas of knowledge
Requires the person in charge to answer on the spot across 18 areas

blocks.text: The areas in 2-102.11(C) include the link between employee hygiene and foodborne disease, exclusion and restriction of ill employees, cooking, cooling, hot holding and reheating temperatures for time/temperature control for safety food, cross contamination and bare hand contact, major food allergens, cleaning and sanitizing, toxic materials, critical control points and HACCP plans, and the rights and responsibilities of employees, the person in charge and the regulatory authority.

sections.heading: Which food protection manager certifications count?

blocks.text: Section 2-102.20 deems a person in charge compliant with 2-102.11(B), and the establishment compliant with 2-102.12, when the certification program is evaluated and listed by a Conference for Food Protection (CFP) recognized accrediting agency as conforming to the CFP Standard for Accreditation of Food Protection Manager Certification Programs.

Annex 3 of the 2026 edition explains that in 2002 the CFP entered a cooperative agreement with the ANSI National Accreditation Board (ANAB) to accredit certification bodies, and ANAB published its first list of accredited certifiers in 2003. A footnote clarifies that "accredited program" refers to the certification examination, not to training or educational programs, so a course certificate alone does not satisfy 2-102.12.

The Food Code itself does not set a validity period for the certificate. Recertification intervals are set by the certifying programs and by the adopting jurisdictions, so an operator should record the expiry date printed on each certificate and any local renewal rule.

sections.heading: What training must the person in charge ensure for other employees?

blocks.text: Section 2-103.11 makes the person in charge responsible for active managerial control, including ensuring that employees are properly trained in food safety, including food allergy awareness, as it relates to their duties (paragraph O). The 2026 edition added paragraph R, requiring employees to be aware of food defense, such as signs of intentional adulteration, and to report suspicious activity.

Paragraph P also requires food employees and conditional employees to be informed in a verifiable manner of their duty to report illness and related information. "Verifiable" points toward a signed acknowledgment or recorded briefing rather than a poster alone. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How can an operator map Food Code duties to evidence?

blocks.text: An operator can map each Food Code duty to the role, the frequency and the record an inspector would look for, then adjust for the local code. The table is illustrative and assumes a jurisdiction that has adopted the 2026 edition without amendment.

blocks.text: Multi state chains should hold one matrix per jurisdiction, because the adopted edition and certification rules differ. See [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations). Food manufacturers face different federal rules, covered under [FSMA preventive controls qualified individual training](/regulations/fsma-preventive-controls-qualified-individual-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can hold the 2-102.11(C) knowledge areas as a structured framework, so internal assessments for shift leads map to the same areas an inspector may question, and each jurisdiction's adopted edition is recorded against the site. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Is a food handler card the same as food protection manager certification?
faqs.a: No. Under section 2-102.20, food protection manager certification means passing an examination from a program accredited to the Conference for Food Protection standard. The Food Code's annex notes that "accredited program" refers to the certification exam, not to training or educational programs. Food handler cards, where required, come from state or local rules.

faqs.q: Does every restaurant need a certified manager on every shift?
faqs.a: Under the model code, a person in charge must be present during all hours of operation and that person must be a certified food protection manager, unless the regulatory authority deems the establishment minimal risk. Adopting jurisdictions can modify this, so the local code decides.

faqs.q: Which Food Code edition applies in my state?
faqs.a: It depends on what your state, territory, county or city has adopted. FDA publishes the model code and maintains Food Code adoption reports, but adoption happens on each jurisdiction's own timetable, so the 2026 edition released on September 17, 2026 will not apply everywhere at once.

faqs.q: What changed for managers in the 2026 Food Code?
faqs.a: FDA's summary of changes says the 2026 edition added a food defense knowledge area at 2-102.11(C)(18) and a new 2-103.11(R) on employee food defense awareness, and revised the lead in to 2-103.11 to emphasize active managerial control. Section 2-102.12 itself was not listed as changed.
